extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in mathematics education (teacher educators, curriculum designers, educational researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, implementing, and evaluating classroom-based interventions and curricular resources to improve students' understanding and practice of mathematical proof across educational levels and mathematical domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Lakatosian/ill-defined tasks to support reinvention
rubrics_metrics.description: Design instruction so students work with definitions and conjectures that are not fully understood by them or are sometimes intentionally imprecisely formulated by the instructor (cf. Lakatos’ methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students may arrive with both a proof and a counterexample; this apparent paradox can be used to clarify definitions, refine conjectures, or analyze proofs for hidden assumptions, thereby motivating construction of new mathematical knowledge. The production and analysis of arguments (even invalid ones) should be treated as integral to creation and modification of concepts, definitions, and conjectures (Larsen & Zandieh, 2008).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving as a socially‑embedded activity (establishing classroom norms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orient interventions toward proving as socially embedded: establish norms and practices in the classroom that invite participation and align settling mathematical arguments with community standards of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include negotiating norms in calculus classes (Alibert & Thomas, 1991), inviting high school students to participate in proof through teacher-established norms (Goos, 2004), and interventions like Mariotti’s that emphasize social negotiation. Teacher facilitation of class discussions is crucial and a focus for preservice teacher training (Stylianides et al., 2013).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving as problem‑solving (teaching processes and heuristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design interventions that teach students processes and heuristics believed to lead to successful proof-writing and proof construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies in this perspective directly teach processes/heuristics (e.g., Anderson et al., 1995; Weber, 2006; Schoenfeld, 1985). Cognitive tutors like the Geometry Tutor have shown large gains (students’ proof-writing ability improving by more than a standard deviation). Self‑explanation training can improve proof comprehension (Hodds, Alcock, & Inglis, 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving as convincing (developing critical attitude toward empirical evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop students’ ability to view proof as convincing rather than relying solely on empirical evidence; foster skepticism that empirical examples alone validate generalizations while still using experiments to develop ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions (e.g., Stylianides & Stylianides, 2009b; Brown, 2014) can help students develop skepticism toward empirical evidence as basis for validation while retaining empirical exploration for generating proof ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design interventions for under‑studied proof methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Create interventions targeted at proof methods that have received less attention (proof by contradiction, contraposition, and counterexample) and design them to address related methods concurrently or separately with adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such interventions should help students develop abilities to refute claims or show that negation leads to contradiction. One approach is to transfer key features of successful induction interventions (e.g., Harel’s notion of 'intellectual need') to these other methods to achieve efficient teaching and help students connect methods and domains (Antonini & Mariotti, 2008).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and principles for teaching axiomatic structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop principles about engaging students in axiomatic structures (axioms, assumptions, definitions, theorems) and investigate whether instruction should start from particular axioms/definitions or from problems that raise the need for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current research focuses heavily on secondary geometry and dynamic geometry environments; open questions include: Is one starting point preferable, in what settings, for which learning goals? Can a set of principles apply across domains (algebra, geometry) and educational levels, and in both technological and non‑technological environments?

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce expandable, developmentally appropriate proof criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide students of different ages with an appropriate set of criteria for judging whether an argument meets the standard of proof; criteria must be elastic/adaptable to students' level without compromising mathematical accuracy or future learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For consistency across levels and domains, the set of proof criteria should be sufficiently elastic to adapt to students’ current knowledge yet preserve mathematical rigor. The chapter’s definition of proof (Stylianides, 2007b) has been adapted for secondary students and preservice teachers and may be further adapted for elementary levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interventions must be both effective and well‑theorized
rubrics_metrics.description: Design interventions that not only achieve intended learning outcomes but are theoretically articulated to illuminate mechanisms of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By clearly articulating the 'theoretically essential components' (aspects presumed to engineer/support intended learning outcomes), interventions become easier to adapt and apply in other classrooms. Theory-rich interventions increase potential for transfer and scaling (Stylianides & Stylianides, 2013; Yeager & Walton, 2011).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design educative curricular resources to support teacher and student learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop curricular materials that promote teacher learning alongside student learning to support broad dissemination of promising interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educative curriculum resources (Ball & Cohen, 1996; Davis & Krajcik, 2005; Stylianides, 2008c) help reduce variation in quality of learning opportunities across classrooms and facilitate scaling of interventions. Well‑designed resources can aid teacher enactment and sustain deep instructional change (Coburn, 2003).

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate scalability and mechanisms for broad dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: When developing interventions, plan for scaling up by specifying which components produce change and how they can be adapted to other settings for deep and lasting impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scaling requires moving beyond successful small trials to thinking about adaptation, teacher learning, and systemic features that support sustained implementation (Coburn, 2003). Articulating mechanisms of success aids adaptation and wider application.
